analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans oil and gas drilling in federal waters off the New England coast.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan New England delegation's bill to ban offshore oil and gas drilling off their states never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written a permanent ban into federal law against leasing any federal waters off Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut for oil or gas drilling. It was introduced with the backing of nearly the entire New England House delegation after the administration proposed opening previously protected Atlantic waters to drilling. The bill never got a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities in Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut, whose economies depend on fishing, tourism, and clean beaches, would gain a permanent legal shield against offshore oil and gas drilling off their shores [S2][S3]. Commercial fishermen would be protected from drilling activity, seismic surveys, and spill risk in the waters where they work. The roughly 20 House members from these states who backed the bill sought this protection for their districts [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: New England coastal communities and fisheries

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have barred the Interior Department from issuing any lease for oil or gas exploration, development, or production off the coasts of Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut, overriding any other law to the contrary.
A statutory ban is permanent protection: unlike a presidential withdrawal or a leasing plan, it could not be reversed by a future administration's five-year drilling plan.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies, which would have been permanently barred from leasing any federal waters off the five New England states for exploration or drilling [S2][S3]. Taxpayers and the federal treasury would forgo any lease revenue if commercial quantities of oil or gas were ever found there, though no active leases or known producing fields existed off New England.

drawbacks.text: A permanent ban would put New England's federal waters permanently off limits to energy development, forgoing any potential lease revenue and domestic oil and gas production from those areas, which supporters of drilling argued the country should not rule out sight unseen.
The bill addressed only New England, leaving the question of Atlantic offshore drilling elsewhere unresolved, so even if enacted it would have been a regional fix rather than a national policy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered permanent, enforceable protection for New England's coastal waters and the fishing and tourism economies that depend on them, at the cost of foreclosing a hypothetical future source of domestic oil and gas about which no company held existing leases. The main cost was opportunity forgone rather than a burden on anyone today, which makes the trade-off relatively favorable to the public, though the permanent nature of the ban means it closes off options even if future conditions or technology changed the calculus.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its energy subcommittee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and never got a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill would have amended the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Department from issuing any lease for oil or gas exploration, development, or production off the coasts of Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut.
It was introduced on January 11, 2018 by Representative Cicilline with 20 cosponsors, 19 Democrats and 1 Republican, drawn entirely from the five New England states.
It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, then to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee five days later, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The oil and gas industry is better off: the legal ban never happened, so federal waters off New England remained legally available for future leasing under whatever plan the Interior Department adopts. New England's coastal communities got no new protection beyond what existing policy happened to provide.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas industry kept future leasing options

for.name: David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban oil and gas leasing off the New England coast.

for.role: 20 House cosponsors from Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; 19 Democrats and 1 Republican signed on, covering all six New England states.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: House Committee on Natural Resources (Republican majority)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced, referred it to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Offshore drilling advocates
against.what_they_did: Supported expanding offshore drilling, including previously protected Atlantic waters, putting the industry's interest at odds with the bill's ban.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 20 cosponsors were almost entirely Democrats, 19 of 20, with a single Republican from Maine, and the Republican-controlled Natural Resources Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have foreclosed any future leasing off New England, keeping those waters off limits to drilling companies. In this fight the industry's interest in access ran against the coastal communities' interest in protection.

The bill would have protected the fishing grounds and coastal waters off New England from drilling activity and spill risk, and no lease revenue was at stake since no active New England leases existed.
Beaches and coastal economies in the five states would have gained a statutory guarantee that drilling could not be authorized offshore.
